newsitem.title: BELGIUM: SHIPPERS TO TRY TO END ANTWERP SOYA PROTEST.
newsitem.headline: SHIPPERS TO TRY TO END ANTWERP SOYA PROTEST.

text.p: Cargill Benelux, the subsidiary of a U.S. grains multinational, said on Friday it would try to end a protest by environmentalist group Greenpeace that has held up a soybeans cargo at the Port of Antwerp for 15 hours.
Greenpeace activists say they are blocking the shipment because it is believed to contain soybeans that have been genetically modified.
"Greenpeace is calling on Cargill to demand the segregation of the soya and to reject further shipments of the genetically engineered beans," the enviornmentalists said in a statement.
But Willem Mock, president of Cargill Benelux, a subsidiary of Cargill Inc, told Reuters it would not give in to Greenpeace's demands.
"We are discussing with local authorities how to gain access to the port. We are also looking at a civil (legal) procedure," he said.

Greenpeace has tied a rubber dinghy to the rudder of the Cargill-chartered bulk carrier, the Polish-registerd Ziemia Zamojska, to prevent it getting through one of Antwerp Port's four sea locks. Activists also chained themselves to the entrance to the lock.
A spokesman for Antwerp Harbourmasters' Office said, however, the action was not greatly affecting other traffic at Europe's second busiest port.
"We put the ship in the smallest lock we have so that consequences for other traffic would be very small," he told Reuters.
Amsterdam-based Greenpeace International has vowed to keep up a campaign of direct action against the imports.
A protest earlier in the week against what was believed to be the first genetic soya shipment in Hamburg, Germany, ended peacefully after police intervened.
Every week in Europe thousands of tonnes of soybeans are processed into meal and oil, which is used in a wide variety of everyday foods such as margarine, chocolate and mayonnaise.
Some leading European firms, including the German unit of Anglo-Dutch Unilever, have bowed to consumer pressure and announced they will not use the new variety even though they consider it safe.
